text: The rate of reaction can be increased by:
sourceFile: Year 10 Chemistry End of Topic Test (Draft 2).docx
html: The rate of reaction can be increased by:
answerHtml:
Worked solution

Heating increases particles’ average kinetic energy, so collisions are more frequent and a larger fraction exceed the activation energy. More successful collisions per second increase the rate.

Marking guidance

Award 1 mark for A. Use the explanation above to check the reasoning.
options: Lowering the pressure on the reactants
Lowering the temperature on the products

text: An antacid tablet is dropped into each of two glasses containing equal amounts of water. The temperature of the water s 50°C in glass 1 and 10°C in glass 2. In each glass, bubbles of gas are released as the tablet dissolves. It takes 30 seconds for the tablet to react completely in glass 1 and 100 seconds for the tablet to react in glass 2. From these results alone we can conclude that:
sourceFile: Year 10 Chemistry End of Topic Test (Draft 2).docx
html: An antacid tablet is dropped into each of two glasses containing equal amounts of water. The temperature of the water s 50°C in glass 1 and 10°C in glass 2. In each glass, bubbles of gas are released as the tablet dissolves. It takes 30 seconds for the tablet to react completely in glass 1 and 100 seconds for the tablet to react in glass 2. From these results alone we can conclude that:
answerHtml:
Worked solution

The same tablet reacts in 30 s in hot water rather than 100 s in cold water. Its average rate is therefore about 100/30 = 3.33 times greater. These results alone do not establish a doubling per 10°C.

Marking guidance

Award 1 mark for D. Use the explanation above to check the reasoning.

Increasing the volume of water increase the rate at which the antacid tablet reacts with water.
The rate of chemical reactions doubles for every 10°C increase in temperature.
The rate at which the antacid tablet reacts with water is faster in hot water than in cold water.

sourceFile: Year 10 Chemistry End of Topic Test (Draft 2).docx
html: Magnesium reacts very rapidly with oxygen once it is ignited, and the reaction gives out a great deal of light energy. Magnesium, in a powdered form, was once used in photography to provide light at the instant that a photo was taken. The reason for using magnesium in a powdered form was most likely:
answerHtml:
Worked solution

Powder exposes a greater surface area for the same mass, allowing more magnesium particles to contact oxygen and react at once.

sourceFile: Year 10 Chemistry End of Topic Test (Draft 2).docx
html:
Explain why propane has 8 hydrogen atoms, but propene has 6. Use a diagram to help your explanation.

[3]
answerHtml:
Worked solution

Propane is CH₃–CH₂–CH₃, C₃H₈, with only single C–C bonds. [1] Propene is CH₂=CH–CH₃, C₃H₆. [1] The double C–C bond uses an extra bonding position on each of two carbons, leaving two fewer positions for H while each C retains four bonds. [1]

text: Lead nitrate reacts with sodium iodide to form a yellow lead iodide precipitate: Pb(NO₃)₂( ) + 2NaI( ) → PbI₂( ) + 2NaNO₃( ). (a) Add state symbols. [2] (b) Why use coefficients to balance the equation? [2] (c) If 2 mol lead nitrate reacts completely, how much lead iodide forms in moles? [1] (d) Calculate its mass. [2]
sourceFile: Year 10 Chemistry End of Topic Test (Draft 2).docx
html: Lead nitrate reacts with sodium iodide to form a yellow lead iodide precipitate: Pb(NO₃)₂( ) + 2NaI( ) → PbI₂( ) + 2NaNO₃( ). (a) Add state symbols. [2] (b) Why use coefficients to balance the equation? [2] (c) If 2 mol lead nitrate reacts completely, how much lead iodide forms in moles? [1] (d) Calculate its mass. [2]
answerHtml:
Worked solution

(a) Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2NaI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq). [2; ½ per state] PbI₂ is the insoluble precipitate.

(b) Atoms are conserved. Coefficients match the number of each atom without changing the identity of a substance; changing subscripts changes the substance. [2]

(c) The mole ratio is 1:1, so 2 mol Pb(NO₃)₂ produces 2 mol PbI₂. [1]

(d) M(PbI₂) = 207.2 + 2(126.9) = 461.0 g mol⁻¹. m = nM = 2 × 461.0 = 922 g. [2]

Marking guidance

Maximum 7 marks. The part allocations are shown with the worked steps above. Accept scientifically equivalent explanations and valid alternative methods; retain units and appropriate directions in calculations.
